title: Evaluating vision-capable chatbots in interpreting kinematics graphs: a comparative study of free and subscription-based models
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how well commercially available vision-capable large multimodal model (LMM) chatbots can interpret kinematics graphs, a foundational visual representation used in physics and more broadly in STEM and medical fields. The authors frame the problem as an educationally important one because these tools are increasingly promoted for tutoring and other educational uses, yet their actual ability to read and reason about graphical information is not well understood. The study asks whether subscription-based chatbots outperform free ones, whether some categories of graph-interpretation tasks are systematically easier or harder for chatbots, and how OpenAI’s vision-capable models have changed over time.

The approach was a comparative benchmark study using the Test of Understanding Graphs in Kinematics (TUG-K), a 26-item multiple-choice concept inventory. Eight chatbots were tested: four freely available (Copilot, Gemini 1.0 Pro, Claude 3 Sonnet, and ChatGPT-4o) and four subscription-based or premium-access models (ChatGPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.0 Ultra, and Gemini 1.5 Pro API). Each item was submitted 30 times to each model using screenshots of the test items, producing 780 responses per chatbot. The researchers coded final answer choices quantitatively and also examined performance patterns across item types and across versions of ChatGPT.

The study did not involve human learners as participants; instead, the chatbots themselves were the units being evaluated in an online testing context. The educational context is therefore indirect: the authors position the findings as relevant for STEM and medical education, especially for graph interpretation, tutoring, assessment, and accessibility applications. The work was conducted by researchers at Uppsala University in Sweden, but the evaluated systems were public AI tools rather than an institutional classroom intervention.

The main conclusion is that subscription-based access did not generally produce better performance. ChatGPT-4o, a freely available model, performed best overall and outperformed even subscription-based ChatGPT-4. OpenAI’s models substantially outperformed the other chatbot families, while Gemini and Claude variants often performed near guessing level. Across task types, chatbots tended to do better on items relying more on linguistic reasoning than on items requiring stronger visual interpretation, and comparing areas under graphs was especially difficult. The authors caution that even the best-performing chatbot remained far from expert level and still made unpredictable errors, limiting its appropriateness for high-stakes educational uses such as grading, tutoring, or exam assistance.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s family of large multimodal chatbot models with vision capabilities for interpreting uploaded images and generating text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated on the Test of Understanding Graphs in Kinematics (TUG-K) to assess vision-capable chatbot performance in interpreting kinematics graphs; versions tested included Gemini 1.0 Pro, Gemini 1.0 Ultra, and Gemini 1.5 Pro API.

findings.finding_summary: Gemini models performed poorly overall on the TUG-K, with Gemini 1.0 Pro averaging 18.8% correct, Gemini 1.0 Ultra averaging 15.6% correct, and Gemini 1.5 Pro API averaging 34.7% correct across 26 items with 30 repetitions per item. Contrary to expectations, the subscription-based Gemini 1.0 Ultra performed worse than the freely available Gemini 1.0 Pro, while Gemini 1.5 Pro API improved over both but still trailed ChatGPT-4 (42.4%) and ChatGPT-4o (58.6%).
findings.measure: Percentage correct on the Test of Understanding Graphs in Kinematics (TUG-K)

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s family of large multimodal chatbot models capable of processing image inputs and producing text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated on the TUG-K for visual interpretation of kinematics graphs; versions tested included Claude 3 Sonnet and Claude 3 Opus.

findings.finding_summary: Claude models showed low TUG-K performance overall, with Claude 3 Sonnet averaging 17.9% correct and Claude 3 Opus averaging 22.8% correct across 26 items with 30 repetitions each. The subscription-based Claude 3 Opus only marginally outperformed the freely available Claude 3 Sonnet, indicating little practical advantage for the premium version on this graph-interpretation task.
findings.measure: Percentage correct on the Test of Understanding Graphs in Kinematics (TUG-K)

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s family of large language and multimodal chatbot models, including vision-capable versions that can interpret uploaded images and respond conversationally.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated on the TUG-K to assess and compare vision-capable chatbot performance in interpreting kinematics graphs; versions included ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-4o, with additional comparison of ChatGPT-4 across October 2023, April 2024, and April 2024 with Advanced Data Analysis enabled.

findings.finding_summary: OpenAI’s chatbots outperformed all other tested chatbots on the TUG-K. ChatGPT-4 averaged 42.4% correct and ChatGPT-4o averaged 58.6% correct across 26 items with 30 repetitions per item, with ChatGPT-4o showing the best overall performance and exceeding ChatGPT-4 by 16.2 percentage points.
findings.measure: Percentage correct on the Test of Understanding Graphs in Kinematics (TUG-K)

findings.finding_summary: Across OpenAI model updates, ChatGPT-4 performance changed only marginally overall from October 2023 to April 2024, increasing from 41.7% to 42.4% correct, though item-level performance both improved and worsened without a clear pattern. ChatGPT-4o then improved substantially to 58.6% correct, outperforming the April 2024 ChatGPT-4 on 17 of 26 items, including 5 items with gains greater than 50 percentage points.
findings.measure: Percentage correct on the Test of Understanding Graphs in Kinematics (TUG-K) across model versions
findings.effect_size: 0.7 percentage-point difference (Oct 2023 vs Apr 2024 ChatGPT-4); 16.2 percentage-point difference (Apr 2024 ChatGPT-4 vs ChatGPT-4o)

findings.finding_summary: Enabling Advanced Data Analysis (ADA) in ChatGPT-4 did not improve overall TUG-K performance. ChatGPT-4 with ADA averaged 40.9% correct versus 42.4% without ADA, and ADA was used automatically in 70% of responses for 6 of 26 items but often ineffectively; 66.7% of responses that used ADA were coded as not answered (N).
findings.measure: Percentage correct on the Test of Understanding Graphs in Kinematics (TUG-K); proportion of ADA-used responses coded not answered

identified_tools.name: Microsoft Copilot
identified_tools.description: Microsoft’s vision-capable chatbot interface built on GPT-family models for conversational responses to text and image inputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated on the TUG-K as a freely available vision-capable chatbot to assess performance in interpreting kinematics graphs.

findings.finding_summary: Microsoft Copilot performed only slightly above guessing on the TUG-K, averaging 25.8% correct across 26 items with 30 repetitions per item. Although based on GPT-4-family technology, it performed far below ChatGPT-4 (42.4%) and ChatGPT-4o (58.6%), which the authors attribute to differences in application-level adaptations such as fine-tuning and system prompts.
findings.measure: Percentage correct on the Test of Understanding Graphs in Kinematics (TUG-K)

quality_tier_rationale: This is an original empirical benchmark study comparing chatbot outputs on a concept inventory, but it is not an intervention study with student participants or causal educational design. The methodology is systematic and transparent, yet evidence is limited to tool performance on test items rather than demonstrated learner outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial differences in chatbot task performance, especially favoring ChatGPT-4o, but does not estimate impact on actual students, teaching, or institutional outcomes. Educational implications are therefore suggestive rather than directly demonstrated.
